opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there's something to it, though I'd frame it less as literal physical hunger and more as the feeling of not being comfortable. When you're a little hungry, in the broad sense, you're more alert, more driven, more willing to grind. When everything is too comfortable, it's easy to coast.

In research I've noticed the people who do the best work usually have this restlessness. They're never quite satisfied with the current result. They want to know why something works, or why it doesn't, and they'll stay up running one more experiment because they can't let it go. That's intellectual hunger, and I think it often comes from having had to fight for things at some point, whether that's resources, recognition, or just a seat at the table.

Comfort is a bit of a trap. Once you're in a big organization with lots of compute and everything is handed to you, there's a risk of losing that edge. So I try to keep that underdog mentality even when things are going well, staying a bit paranoid and assuming there's always something more to learn or someone out there doing it better.

But I wouldn't romanticize actual suffering. Starving yourself doesn't make you a better scientist. It's more about keeping an appetite: being curious, a bit dissatisfied, and hungry to understand things more deeply. That's the part worth cultivating.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'm a bit skeptical of it as a literal claim. I don't think being hungry makes you smarter or more curious in any direct way. If anything, when you're actually hungry, you just think about food.

But I think there's a version of it that's true, and it's more about scarcity and chips on shoulders. A lot of the people I've seen do really well in research, especially people who came up outside the usual Stanford or Berkeley pipeline, had something to prove. I did my PhD in Singapore, which is not exactly where people expect top ML research to come from. For a long time I felt like I had to work harder just to get noticed, to get reviewers to take a paper seriously, to get people at Google to even read what I was doing. That kind of hunger is real, and it compounds. You publish more, you read more, you're always slightly uncomfortable, and that discomfort pushes you.

The problem is that it's easy to romanticize. Plenty of people go through hardship and it just burns them out. And plenty of people with very comfortable lives are incredibly intellectually driven because they just love the problems. So I don't think deprivation is the mechanism. I think the mechanism is caring about something enough that you can't let it go, and sometimes being an outsider happens to produce that feeling.

If I'm being honest about my own case, the drive was less about physical hunger and more about not wanting to be irrelevant. That fear of being left behind, especially in a field that moves this fast, is a much stronger motivator for me than anything else. Whether that's healthy is a separate question.

r001.rationale: The candidate says that when someone is actually hungry, they just think about food, rejecting a direct link between physical hunger and intellectual curiosity.

astra-6.text: I think there’s something to that, but I wouldn’t take it too literally. If you’re physically hungry, it can be hard to think about anything else. So I don’t think deprivation is a prerequisite for intellectual ambition. But the broader experience of wanting something you don’t have—of having to work toward it—can give you a certain drive. The interesting question is whether that drive survives once you’re comfortable. Can curiosity keep you hungry even when you don’t have anything left to prove?

r001.rationale: The response says that when physically hungry, it can be hard to think about anything else, conveying that hunger pulls attention away toward food.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t think you need to experience physical hunger to develop intellectual hunger. Adversity can give you a strong drive to change your circumstances, but it can also make it much harder to think, explore, and take risks. If you’re worried about your next meal, you don’t necessarily have the space to pursue an interesting research question.

For me, the more useful distinction is between being comfortable and becoming complacent. You can have your basic needs met and still feel that there’s so much you don’t understand, so much you want to build. That kind of hunger can come from curiosity. I’d rather we help people develop that than suggest they need to suffer first.
